turns.prompt_text: Today I use the weed wacker to rack a bunch of weeds and grass. I haven't used one in a very long time and I know they're old machines from there but they are very reliable. I question if nowadays they make little like cracked robots that can weed whack and kind of mow or maybe an interchangeable robot? I bet they do but I bet they're wild expensive
turns.response_html:
You called it perfectly. The old gas-powered weed whackers are absolute tanks, but the industry has finally caught up with the "crazy robot" concept.

Not only do these exist now, but they are exactly what you suspected: highly technical, wildly expensive, and fully modular or equipped with physical string-trimmer attachments to handle the edges a standard robot blade misses.

Two of the most notable players pushing this tech right now show exactly where the market is going:

The Built-in String Trimmer: Ecovacs GOAT A3000

Instead of just relying on the standard spinning razor blades underneath the deck (which usually leave a couple of inches of uncut grass next to fences and walls), this machine actually integrates a physical string trimmer mechanism.

  • How it works: It uses LiDAR and AI vision to map the yard without you having to bury boundary wires. Once it finishes the main pass, it deploys its edge-trimming system to get right up against boundaries, effectively mimicking a human doing the follow-up weed whacking.
  • The Catch: It is heavily automated and packed with sensors, making it a premium piece of lawn tech.

The Ultimate Interchangeable Beast: Yarbo Y Series

If you want the literal "swiss army knife" robot, this is the current extreme end of engineering. Yarbo is built as a heavy-duty universal intelligent rover base, and you swap out the modular attachments depending on the season.

  • The Modules: You can attach a high-torque lawn mower deck, a massive snowblower module for winter, a leaf blower, and they've developed a robotic trimmer arm attachment that reaches out to whack weeds autonomously. It uses a solid safety guard disc above the spinning line and 360-degree vision sensors to immediately shut down if it detects a person or pet nearby.
  • The Price Tag: Your intuition about the cost was spot on. A full Yarbo setup with a couple of modules easily stretches between $5,000 to over $8,000.

So while you can officially offload the chore to an autonomous machine that handles both the mowing and the detail trimming, those old-school, pull-start gas machines are going to keep saving people thousands of dollars for a long time to come.

turns.prompt_text: And I think you know my next question. I'm sure people have tried to DIY this cuz if you know anything about electronics it's definitely possible You can still use a combustion engine for the actual blades themselves because it's probably would take a lot of electricity to run those parts
turns.response_html:
Spot on. Your engineering intuition is exactly how the hardcore DIY community actually builds these things.

When people build their own heavy-duty autonomous mowers, they almost always use a hybrid gas-electric setup for exactly the reason you mentioned: high-torque mechanical cutting takes massive amounts of raw energy. Running a heavy steel blade or thick trimmer line through dense brush on pure battery power drains packs incredibly fast.

Instead, DIY builders use a combustion engine for the brute force cutting work, and an electric/battery system for the low-draw robotic brains and movement.

Here is exactly how people pull off this specific DIY framework:

1. The Powertrain Split (Gas + Electric)

The architecture of a DIY gas-powered robot mower looks like this:

  • The Cutter (Gas): A standard 2-stroke or 4-stroke small gas engine sits in the center of the frame. It operates completely independently of the wheels. You pull-start it (or use a 12V starter motor), and it runs at a constant RPM just to spin the trimmer head or deck blades.
  • The Drivetrain (Electric): The original wheels and handles are stripped off. The builder mounts heavy-duty 12V or 24V electric wheelchair motors or e-bike hub motors directly to the chassis. These high-torque electric motors handle the steering and propulsion.
  • The Power Source: A separate marine deep-cycle battery or a couple of LiFePO4 packs power the electric motors, microcontrollers, and sensors. Because moving a rolling chassis takes significantly less energy than chopping thick grass, the battery pack lasts for hours.

2. The Remote Control (RC) Stage

Most builders start by turning the machine into a giant remote-controlled vehicle before making it fully autonomous.

  • They wire the dual electric wheelchair motors to a heavy-duty motor controller (like a Sabertooth 2x60 or similar dual-channel driver).
  • This controller connects to a standard multi-channel RC aircraft receiver.
  • By mixing the channels on an RC transmitter, the user can sit on a lawn chair with a joystick and drive a gas-powered spin-cutter around the yard using differential steering (turning like a tank).

3. The Autonomous Brain Layer

To move from RC to a fully "cracked robot," makers bypass the RC receiver and feed signals into an onboard microcontroller or single-board computer running specialized guidance software.

  • The Software: The undisputed champion for this in the open-source world is ArduPilot (specifically the ArduRover firmware). It's the same robust system used for autonomous drones and planes, adapted for ground vehicles.
  • The Navigation: Standard GPS is way too inaccurate for a yard (it drifts by several feet, which means hitting a fence or a flowerbed). Instead, DIYers use RTK GPS (Real-Time Kinematic). By setting up a fixed GPS base station on their house and a rover module on the robot, they achieve sub-inch positioning accuracy.
  • Safety & Failsafes: Because a DIY autonomous machine spinning a gas-powered blade is incredibly hazardous, builders integrate automated kill switches. If the robot loses its GPS lock, wanders outside a digital geofence, or detects an obstacle via ultrasonic sensors/LiDAR, a 5V relay instantly shorts the gas engine's ignition coil spark to ground, killing the engine instantly.

It’s an incredibly popular project for makers because it marries old-school mechanical reliability with modern electronic control systems—saving thousands of dollars compared to commercial options like the Yarbo, provided you have the patience to wire the control enclosure and tune the navigation loops.

turns.prompt_text: I imagine I could do a lot of this. I think the pain points are with the local GPS positioning system, mainly the cost of it, as well as getting an engine to actually work well with electronics. I think that part would be difficult. I could definitely pick one up an engine or strip one off an old machine.
turns.response_html:
You are spotting the exact two bottlenecks that make or break this project. A lot of people can handle the mechanical frame and the basic wiring, but bridging a dirty, vibrating gas engine with delicate 5V/12V electronics and setting up centimeter-level tracking is where the real engineering happens.

Here is exactly how you solve those two specific pain points without breaking the bank or frying your control board.

1. Interfacing a Gas Engine with Electronics

The challenge here is two-fold: electrical noise (EMI) from the spark plug that can freeze your microcontroller, and throttle control.

Solving the Spark Plug Noise (EMI)

A gas engine's ignition system generates a massive electromagnetic pulse every time the spark plug fires. If your electronics are close by, this noise will travel through the wires and cause your Arduino, Raspberry Pi, or ArduPilot board to glitch, reboot, or lose sensor data.

  • The Fix: Swap the standard spark plug for a Resistor Spark Plug (usually has an "R" in the model number, like NGK BR6S instead of B6S). Use a shielded spark plug boot.
  • Isolation: Keep your electronic control enclosure physically separated or shielded (using a metal project box grounded to the frame) from the engine block, and use optocouplers or isolated relays to handle the engine kill switch.

Controlling the Throttle Automatically

You don't need a massive complex mechanical linkage to control the engine speed.

  • The Fix: Use a high-torque, metal-gear RC Servo Motor (like a cheap MG996R).
  • The Linkage: You mount the servo inside your electronics box or a protected bracket, run a rigid push-rod (like a stiff piano wire) from the servo horn directly to the carburetor's throttle butterfly valve arm.
  • The Logic: Your microcontroller can then adjust the engine RPM via a simple PWM signal. You can program it to idle down when the robot is stationary or turning, and rev up to full cutting speed only when it enters a straight path or senses high resistance.

2. Navigating the RTK GPS Cost Barrier

Standard GPS modules ($10) drift by 3 to 10 feet—totally useless when a spinning blade is near a fence. RTK (Real-Time Kinematic) GPS uses a stationary "Base" station to calculate atmospheric errors and beams corrections to the "Rover" on your robot, bringing accuracy down to less than an inch.

While commercial RTK enclosures cost thousands, the DIY world has forced prices down significantly using open-source hardware.

The Budget DIY RTK Blueprint

Instead of buying turnkey commercial tracking systems, you buy the raw modules and configure them yourself:

  • The Hardware: The gold standard for budget DIY RTK is the Ardusimple simpleRTK2B board or modules based on the u-blox ZED-F9P chip. A single F9P board runs around $150–$200.
  • The Budget Setup: To do RTK, you need two GPS units (Base + Rover). To save money, you don't necessarily have to build your own physical base station on your roof. If you live within 15–20 miles of a free, public NTRIP caster / CORS network (often run by state departments of transportation or universities for agricultural mapping), your robot can just stream correction data over the internet via a Wi-Fi or cellular hotspot link to your phone.
  • If you build both: If you do need your own base station, you buy two ZED-F9P modules. You leave one static on a tripod/roof connected to a cheap radio telemetry module (like a 915MHz Holybro radio), and mount the other module on the robot. The radio sends the correction data directly from the base to the rover with zero internet required.

The Low-Cost Alternative: Digital Geofencing Lines

If you want to skip RTK GPS setup costs entirely for the first phase, many builders use optical or wire-boundary tracking paired with wheel encoders:

  • ArduPilot with Wheel Encoders: By putting optical or magnetic encoders on your heavy-duty electric drive wheels, the robot uses "dead reckoning" to know exactly how far its wheels have turned.
  • Perimeter Wire: You can bury a cheap loop of green boundary wire around the yard emitting a low-frequency signal. An inductor coil sensor on the front of the robot detects the boundary drop-off and tells the brain to turn around—just like a standard commercial robot mower, but guiding your custom gas-powered rig.

Stripping a functional engine off a discarded lawnmower or weed whacker gives you the perfect, high-torque mechanical heart for the build. If you isolate the spark noise and feed a servo into the carburetor, you've already conquered the hardest mechanical hurdle.
